title: The swipe happens before your video gets to the point
markdown:
# The swipe happens before your video gets to the point

At 9:14 p.m., the edit looks finished. The captions are clean. The lighting holds. The video opens with, "Today I want to share three ways to make your product videos better." Two seconds later, a thumb moves on.

The problem is not that the advice was bad. The viewer never got far enough to find out.

Short-form video starts in a hostile little environment: a moving feed, a distracted viewer, and a decision made before an introduction has time to work. A useful hook gives that decision a reason to pause. It does not need to sound dramatic. It needs to make the right person recognize a problem they already have.

## Start where the viewer is stuck

Creators often open from their own side of the camera: "I want to talk about..." or "Here are some tips..." That is accurate, but it leaves the viewer to do the work of figuring out why it matters.

Begin with the moment they know. For a product-video lesson, "If people leave before they see the product, your first sentence is doing the damage" gives the clip a job straight away. For a tutorial, "The useful part of your tutorial arrives too late" is more alive than a summary of what you plan to teach.

The aim is not to accuse people or create fake urgency. It is to name a familiar friction precisely enough that staying feels worthwhile.

## Let the first line earn the second

A hook has one job: earn the next beat. It does not need to explain the whole clip.

Try this shape:

1. Name the friction.
2. Suggest the cause or payoff.
3. Move into the proof.

"Your call to action is not being ignored. Most viewers never reach it." That opening gives the following clip somewhere to go: show the retention dip, then show the change. If the hook needs several sentences of context, it is probably a topic sentence with extra volume. Trim it until the tension lands without your backstory.

## Write options before the camera is on

The opening becomes much harder to fix when it is already buried in an edit. Before recording, write five versions and ask a blunt question of each one: would a stranger know why to keep watching?

For a lesson about showing the result before the process, you might try these angles:

- "Your tutorial loses people before the useful part starts."
- "The edit did not save this video. The first sentence did."
- "I used to open every tutorial with context. Viewers skipped that part."
- "Show the payoff before you explain the steps."
- "This clip has one swipe to make its case."

They are prompts, not formulas. Repeating "Stop doing this" until it becomes your whole personality only teaches regular viewers when to leave. A good candidate sounds like it belongs to this video, not to a pile of videos.

## Check the opening twice

Watch the first three seconds with the sound off. The frame, the on-screen words, and the first action should tell a viewer what is at stake. Then look away and listen. Does the spoken line create a question the next line answers?

There is one more useful test. Remove your name, niche, and existing audience from the equation. Would this still make sense to someone who found you for the first time? Followers may grant you a little patience. New viewers have no reason to.

## Promise only what the clip can deliver

Big promises can buy a pause, then waste it. "This changes everything" gives you almost nothing concrete to show. A smaller promise, such as a line to replace or a before-and-after example, gives the viewer proof early.

Put that proof near the front. If your video teaches a better hook, show the weak opening and the revision before the broader lesson. You are not trying to manufacture a magic phrase. You are moving the useful part forward.

Before the next shoot, write down the thought behind the swipe: "I know this already," "Where is this going?" or "This is not for me." Write five openings that answer one of those thoughts. Read them aloud. Keep the line that makes the next line feel necessary.

If you want a focused workspace for generating, comparing, and sharpening those openings before you record, [Hook Lab](https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog) is made for that job.

The first three seconds do not need to carry the entire video. They only need to make the viewer curious enough to see what you can prove.
